title: From First Principles
text: Recent posts

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
text:
In September 2026 OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra with a table of benchmark results, including 96.0% on GPQA Diamond, 97.6% on FrontierMath Tier 4 (v2), and “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1”. Around the same time Anthropic released Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, each with its own table. Each launch reports higher scores than the one before. The scores keep climbing, and it all looks impressive. But what is actually being tested? Who wrote the test, who graded it, and what does 74.1% mean?
This post opens up the benchmarks behind those tables. We treat a benchmark the way we would treat any measurement in an experiment: a sample of tasks, a procedure, a grader and an average. Seen this way, a benchmark score is an average with a standard error, just like a metric in an AB test, and it has the same kinds of biases. We start by decoding one score, “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1”. Then we tour the benchmarks that recur in launch tables, who made them, and who grades them. Finally we look at when a high score should raise our confidence, and when we should still have doubts.
The numbers in this post are as reported by the model developers and benchmark maintainers as of October 13, 2026, unless noted otherwise.

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
section: What does “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1” mean?
text:
What does “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1” mean?
DeepSWE was built by Datacurve, a company that supplies expert-written coding data, training environments and benchmarks to AI developers.
The tasks. DeepSWE has 113 tasks drawn from 91 open-source repositories, each with at least 500 GitHub stars. The repositories are written in TypeScript, Go, Python, JavaScript and Rust. Software engineers wrote each task from scratch. They came up with the problem, built the environment, wrote and verified the tests, and reviewed each other’s work. A typical task reads like a feature request. One example is adding cancellation support to Boa, a JavaScript engine written in Rust. The reference solutions are large: on average 668 added lines across 7 files.
The harness. The model works as an agent: it gets a copy of the repository and a terminal, and it can read files, run commands and edit code over many steps. For the public leaderboard, Datacurve runs every model in the same simple harness, mini-swe-agent, so that differences come from the model and not from tooling. The model finishes by committing its changes.
The grader. In version 1.1, a fresh container that the agent never touched applies the model’s changes and runs a hidden test suite. The suite contains new tests that check the requested behavior through public interfaces, plus the repository’s existing tests, which check that nothing else broke. No human and no AI reads the code to grade it. The tests do the grading. This setup is what distinguishes version 1.1 from 1.0, which uses the same tasks. Datacurve designed it to make the grader harder to game: an agent cannot patch the test framework inside the grading container, and a test that is dropped or cut short by an early exit shows up as missing or failed rather than passing.
The score. Each task is attempted many times. Datacurve notes that 73 of Claude Fable 5’s 2,260 attempts did not finish, and 2,260 / 113 = 20, so each model gets 20 attempts per task. Datacurve reports pass@1, the probability that a single attempt passes. With 20 attempts per task, a natural estimate takes the share of each task’s attempts whose code passes the hidden tests, then averages that share over all 113 tasks.
So “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1” means: if we give GPT-6 Astra one of these 113 feature requests, its code passes the hidden tests 74.1% of the time on average, the equivalent of about 84 of the 113 tasks.
Who ran it? The 74.1% is OpenAI’s own run. Datacurve also runs Astra on its public leaderboard, in mini-swe-agent at the “xhigh” effort setting, and gets 74% ± 3%. Here the two agree. But a developer’s own run and a run by the benchmark maintainer are different measurements, and they do not always agree.

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
section: Software engineering: can it do a ticket?
text:
Software engineering: can it do a ticket?
Coding benchmarks used to be short puzzles: write a function, pass a few unit tests. Today’s coding benchmarks are agentic. The model gets a whole environment and a vague goal, much like a ticket handed to an engineer.

DeepSWE is described above. On Datacurve’s leaderboard, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Opus 5 are tied at the top at 74%.
Terminal-Bench 4.0 has 66 tasks spanning software, machine learning, science, operations, security, hardware and media. Each task runs in a real terminal, and the grader checks the final state of the machine. The project was started by Stanford and the Laude Institute in 2025. The task set is revised as models catch up: version 4.0 removed 8 tasks from 3.0 and fixed 19 others. Small models still lag far behind here. Anthropic reports Haiku 5.5 at 39.2% against Sonnet 5.5 at 70.6%.

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
section: Science and math: does it know what an expert knows?
text:
Science and math: does it know what an expert knows?

GPQA (“Graduate-level Google-Proof Q&A”) was written by Rein et al. (2023). Domain experts with or pursuing PhDs wrote multiple-choice questions in biology, physics and chemistry. Other experts answered them correctly 65% of the time. Skilled non-experts managed only 34%, despite spending over 30 minutes per question with unrestricted web access. The Diamond subset keeps 198 questions on which the expert validators agreed with the answer key and most non-experts did not. Random guessing among four choices scores 25%. In 2023, the strongest GPT-4-based baseline scored 39%. OpenAI now reports 96.0% for GPT-6 Astra.
Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE), released by the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI in January 2025, has 2,500 questions crowdsourced from experts. About 41% are math, and the rest cover physics, biology, chemistry, computer science, the humanities and more. A question was accepted only if the frontier models of the time failed it, and only after two rounds of expert review. So by construction, the models of early 2025 scored low on it. About three quarters of the answers are short exact answers rather than multiple choice. Anthropic reports Fable 5.1 at 60.9% without tools and 65.0% with tools.
FrontierMath, built by Epoch AI, contains unpublished research-level math problems. Each answer is a number or a mathematical object that a program can check. Tier 4 is the hardest tier. OpenAI reports 97.6% for GPT-6 Astra on Tier 4 (v2).

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
section: Computer use and knowledge work: can it do the job?
text:
Computer use and knowledge work: can it do the job?

OSWorld puts the model in front of a real Ubuntu desktop and asks it to do things like edit a spreadsheet in LibreOffice or change a setting in VS Code. The model sees screenshots and acts with the mouse and keyboard. The original release had 369 tasks, and the 2026 tables use the revised 2.x versions. A script then inspects the computer, for example the file contents or the config, to check that the job was done.
GDPval is a set of 1,320 tasks OpenAI developed in 2025 with industry professionals, spanning 44 occupations in 9 industries: write a memo, build a spreadsheet model, design a slide deck. GDPval-AA is the version run by Artificial Analysis, an independent evaluation company, on 220 of these tasks. The model works as an agent with a shell and web browsing and produces a real deliverable. Unlike everything else in the table, the score is an Elo rating, not a percentage. An AI judge sees two models’ deliverables for the same task, without names, and picks the better one. In version 2.1 the scale is anchored by fixing one reference model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, at 1600. Only differences in Elo carry meaning: a larger gap means a higher expected win rate when two models’ deliverables are compared. Anthropic’s report of Haiku 5.5 at 1620 against Haiku 4.5 at 735 on version 2.1 means the newer model would be expected to win most head-to-head comparisons, not that it gets 1620 of anything right.

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
section: Cybersecurity: can it defend or attack?
text:
Cybersecurity: can it defend or attack?

CWE-bench v1, from Collinear AI, has 120 audit-and-patch tasks covering 73 categories of software weakness (CWEs) in 8 languages. The vulnerabilities are undisclosed, and the agent must find and fix them without breaking existing functionality. This is defensive work.
ExploitBench, from Lee and Brumley at Carnegie Mellon, is offensive. It contains 41 real bugs in V8, the JavaScript engine inside Chrome. Instead of a single pass or fail, it scores a ladder of 16 capabilities: from triggering the bug, through gaining read and write access to memory, up to arbitrary code execution. A deterministic verifier checks each rung. The exploit must work against the buggy version and fail against the patched one.

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
text:
Who runs the exam?
A benchmark is not a sealed exam administered by a testing agency. Most are published openly: the tasks, the grader and often a reference harness are available for anyone to download and run against any model they can access. DeepSWE’s repository contains all 113 tasks with their tests and grader configuration, plus a quickstart that runs the benchmark with Datacurve’s Pier tool. The mini-swe-agent harness that Datacurve uses for its leaderboard is also open source, as is Terminal-Bench. The questions for GPQA and HLE are on Hugging Face; GPQA is gated, so we must request access and accept its terms first. Evaluation frameworks package many benchmarks with a ready-made harness and grader. The UK AI Security Institute’s Inspect Evals includes GPQA, HLE and OSWorld, and EleutherAI’s lm-evaluation-harness covers a wide range of question-and-answer benchmarks.
The model is the other half. Frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 cannot be downloaded: we reach them through their developers’ APIs with an API key, and the harness sends each task to the API. Open-weight models can be downloaded from Hugging Face, for example OpenAI’s gpt-oss-20b, and run on our own hardware. Either way, the same benchmark can be run by several different groups, and a score is only as informative as our knowledge of who ran it and how. Three groups do most of the running.

The model’s developer, in house. Most numbers in a launch table come from the developer’s own evaluation team, running the benchmark on its own infrastructure before release. OpenAI’s launch post says its GPT evaluations “were run in our research environment or via our API”, which “may provide slightly different output from production ChatGPT due to differences in the system prompts, tools available, etc.” The developer chooses the harness and the settings, and OpenAI reports the maximum score at any effort setting. For competitors’ columns, a developer either copies the competitor’s published number, which OpenAI’s charts label “reported score only”, or runs the competitor’s model itself through that competitor’s public API. OpenAI did the latter for HealthBench Professional: “we independently evaluated all Claude models following the intended HealthBench Professional procedure.”
The benchmark’s maintainer. Some maintainers run models themselves and publish a leaderboard. Datacurve runs every model on DeepSWE in the same harness, mini-swe-agent, so that differences come from the models rather than the tooling. This is how we got Datacurve’s 74% ± 3% for Astra, next to OpenAI’s in-house 74.1%. Maintainers sometimes test a model before its launch: OpenAI’s post quotes the ARC Prize Foundation, which maintains ARC-AGI-3, on its own testing of Astra, calling it “the best model we’ve ever tested”.
Independent evaluation organizations. Companies like Artificial Analysis run many benchmarks across many models in one shared setup, and publish the results. They run GDPval-AA, and combined indices such as the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, which OpenAI’s own table reports. They usually test models through the same public API that customers use, and sometimes get access before launch: Anthropic’s Sonnet 5.5 page notes that Artificial Analysis tested a pre-release deployment.

A launch table usually mixes all three, and the footnotes often say which is which. The in-house runs are the most numerous and come with the developer’s choices of harness and settings. The maintainer and independent runs are fewer, but they apply one setup to every model. When an in-house number and an independent number for the same model agree, as Astra’s do on DeepSWE, we learn that the result does not hinge on who ran it.

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
section: Testing a gap with a paired comparison
text:
Testing a gap with a paired comparison
With real data we cannot simulate the null, but we can estimate its spread from a single benchmark run. For each task \(j\), let \(d_j = s_{A,j} - s_{B,j}\) be the difference in the two models’ pass rates. The gap in scores is the average difference,
\[\hat p_A - \hat p_B = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^n d_j = \bar d.\]
If the tasks are a random sample from the population, the \(d_j\) are independent draws, so \(\bar d\) is a sample mean with standard error \(\text{sd}(d_j)/\sqrt{n}\), and \(z = \bar d / (\text{sd}(d_j)/\sqrt{n})\). Each \(d_j\) includes both sources of noise, the task’s difficulty for each model and the randomness of the attempts, so this standard error accounts for both. Pairing matters. A hard task lowers both \(s_{A,j}\) and \(s_{B,j}\), and taking the difference cancels the shared part. This is the same logic as a within-user comparison in an AB test, with tasks in the role of users.
We can test this on one simulated benchmark run, and compare the paired standard error with the spread of the gap across the 2,000 fresh benchmarks. We also compute the unpaired standard error, which treats the two scores as if they came from independent task sets.


Code
set.seed(7)

one_run <- slice_sample(pool, n = n) |>
  mutate(
    s_A = rbinom(n(), K, theta_A) / K,
    s_B = rbinom(n(), K, theta_B) / K,
    d_j = s_A - s_B
  )

paired_test <- one_run |>
  summarise(
    d_bar = mean(d_j),
    se_paired = sd(d_j) / sqrt(n()),
    se_unpaired = sqrt(var(s_A) + var(s_B)) / sqrt(n()),
    z = d_bar / se_paired
  )
paired_test


# A tibble: 1 × 4
     d_bar se_paired se_unpaired      z
     <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>  <dbl>
1 -0.00619    0.0224      0.0346 -0.276


The paired standard error from this one run is 2.2 points, close to the 2.3-point spread of the gap across the fresh benchmarks. The unpaired standard error is 3.5 points. It overstates the noise, because it ignores that both models faced the same tasks. With per-task results for two real models, the same calculation would give a p-value for their gap without any simulation.

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
section: The model may have seen the exam
text:
The model may have seen the exam
Models are trained on large amounts of internet text. If benchmark questions, or their solutions, are on the internet, a model can score well by remembering rather than reasoning. This is called contamination, and it pushes scores up.
ExploitBench shows how contamination can be measured. Its 41 bugs are real V8 vulnerabilities disclosed in 2024 or later. Their descriptions, patches and bug-tracker discussions are public, although working exploits were published for only 2 of them. OpenAI reported that GPT-6 Astra reached arbitrary code execution on all 41, a score of 100%.
In the same launch post, OpenAI raised the question itself: “given concerns that exposure to historical software vulnerabilities may have affected benchmark results”, it also built an internal set of 20 high-severity V8 vulnerabilities disclosed between June and August 2026, after the model’s knowledge cutoff. Astra scored 39.0% on that set, against 5.5% for GPT-5.6 Sol. OpenAI notes that some of these vulnerabilities may not permit arbitrary code execution under the evaluation’s constraints, so 100% may not be achievable there. It also reports that Astra found two previously unknown vulnerabilities during the evaluation, which OpenAI is disclosing to their maintainers.
The two sets contain different bugs, so the scores are not directly comparable. Epoch AI’s review attributes part of the 100% to contamination, and notes that the size of the effect is hard to quantify. For newly disclosed vulnerabilities, the 39.0% is the more direct measurement, and running such a check is what makes the 100% interpretable.
Benchmark maintainers watch for this too. When Terminal-Bench moved to version 4.0, it removed 2 tasks because their solutions had become public.
Exposure can also come from how a benchmark is funded and shared. OpenAI commissioned Epoch AI to produce 300 advanced math problems for FrontierMath, owns them, and has access to the problems and their solutions. Epoch AI also maintains a separate holdout set of 50 problems, for which OpenAI receives only the problem statements, so that every lab’s models can be tested on solutions no lab has seen. When reading a FrontierMath score, it helps to know whether it was measured on the holdout set.

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
section: The answer key can be wrong
text:
The answer key can be wrong
Benchmarks are written by people, and people make mistakes. When the grader is wrong, the error can push scores in either direction.
DeepSWE. Epoch AI reviews popular benchmarks. On September 7, 2026 it rated DeepSWE v1.1 “Flawed”. It found false negatives, where correct work is marked as failing, in at least 23 of the 113 tasks (20.3%). It stopped inspecting once the errors passed its published 20% threshold, so there may be more. 78% of these errors were collisions. The verifier adds its hidden tests to the model’s changes, so when the model had written its own test with the same name as a hidden one, the test package failed to compile. The models had no way to know this and were not told to avoid it. These errors push DeepSWE scores down.
Errors in the other direction have been reported too. On October 2, 2026 an outside audit firm opened a public issue on DeepSWE’s repository showing false positives. A submitted patch can change test infrastructure that the verifier then loads. In one example, a patch that only edited a test configuration file, rewriting failed test reports as passes, received full credit without implementing the feature. As of this writing the issue is open, with no public response from Datacurve.
HLE. In July 2025, FutureHouse reported that 29% ± 3.7% (95% confidence interval) of the answers to HLE’s text-only chemistry and biology questions conflicted with the peer-reviewed literature. That estimate came from 321 questions, checked by FutureHouse’s literature-search agent and validated by expert reviewers on a sample. In September 2025, FutureHouse posted an update: the HLE team’s own review, in which three experts examined each question in a subset of the biology and chemistry questions, found about 18% of them problematic. At least one of the three experts disagreed with the answer in about 25% of cases. The two estimates differ, but both are far from zero. The HLE organizers responded by committing to a rolling revision process for the benchmark.
A wrong answer key puts a ceiling on the score. If a fraction \(w\) of the answer key is wrong, a model that always gives the truly correct answer is marked wrong on those questions and scores at most \(1 - w\). The HLE team found about 18% of the questions they reviewed problematic. If all of those had wrong answers, \(w = 0.18\) and the ceiling on those questions would be 82%. Near the ceiling, we cannot tell a better model from one that better matches the mistakes in the key.

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
section: The harness and settings are part of the score
text:
The harness and settings are part of the score
The same model gets different scores under different harnesses and settings. The differences can be larger than the gaps between models:

On ExploitBench, GPT-5.5 running in OpenAI’s Codex harness reached arbitrary code execution 12 times when allowed 3,000 turns. With a 300-turn limit, it reached it 0 times in the Codex harness and once without it. OpenAI’s launch post makes the same point about its own models: GPT-5.6 Sol’s 5.5% on the June–August set is an artifact of that set’s 300-turn limit, and Sol scored 11.5% at similar settings with fewer limits.
Scores are usually reported at a high “effort” or reasoning budget, which costs more and takes longer than many production settings. OpenAI’s table states that its “evaluation scores are the maximum at any effort”. Anthropic’s footnote for Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 says the reported number is the model’s highest score, obtained at the “xhigh” effort setting.
More effort is not always better. On FrontierCode, a coding benchmark that penalizes changes outside the task’s scope, Sonnet 5.5 scored lower at its maximum effort setting than at xhigh. At maximum effort it ran additional code-review subagents, which occasionally caused timeouts or extra edits.
On OSWorld 2.0 tasks where Anthropic’s production safeguards intervened, Fable 5.1 scored zero. Here the deployment setup lowers the score.

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
section: The same name can mean different scores
text:
The same name can mean different scores
Sonnet 5.5 appears with two different OSWorld 2.1 numbers on Anthropic’s own pages: 80.1% under a “partial” scoring rule on the Sonnet launch page, and 83.9% on an “offline subset” of the tasks on the Haiku launch page. Fable 5.1 is reported at 77.9% on OSWorld 2.0 under the “partial” rule and 41.7% under a “strict” one. Neither number is wrong, but they are different measurements.
Benchmarks also get revised. Terminal-Bench calls version 4.0 a breaking change that requires re-running trials, because it changed both the task set and the resources given to the agent. So a model’s score on 4.0 cannot be compared with an older model’s score on 3.0. Anthropic’s OSWorld 2.0 scores use the benchmark authors’ August 2026 task release, and Anthropic re-ran its older models under the same conditions. That is the right practice, and it is worth checking for whenever a table compares models across versions.

title: What are AI Benchmarks?
section: The benchmark does not represent the consumer’s task
text:
The benchmark does not represent the consumer’s task
Even a perfect benchmark measures the model on its own task distribution. It’s not necessarily what the consumer cares most about. DeepSWE’s tasks are in five languages, from open-source repositories with at least 500 GitHub stars, each with a written task description. The consumer’s codebase may be private, old, underspecified and in a language the benchmark does not cover. A benchmark tells the consumer which models are worth trying. Whether a model improves the consumer’s product is still a causal question about that product’s users, and the final judge is an AB test.

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
text:
In the conditionally sufficient statistics post, a streaming service prompted households to turn on a new playback setting and measured how it changed hours watched and rebuffers per play. One universal model handled everything that made that experiment hard: households with several profiles, a prompt that profiles could ignore, a ramp from 5% to 50% of new accounts, and a ratio metric. It reported each effect with a standard error, and it could do so from a compressed dataset of 8 rows.
The product manager reads the report and asks a different question: what is the probability that the setting cuts rebuffers per play by at least 10% for the profiles that use it? A standard error does not answer that. A posterior distribution does, and in the posterior distribution post we argued that a posterior is what decision makers want. The bootstrap post showed how to get one for a least squares fit without writing a likelihood, with the Bayesian bootstrap.
This post combines the two. We first show that the Bayesian bootstrap gives a posterior for every design the universal model covers, and then that it can be computed in one pass over the data, or from the compressed dataset itself.
The data in this post is synthetic and the scenario is educational. It does not describe a production system.

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
Bayesian Universal Modeling
text:
The model
The universal model is two stage least squares with weights and cluster robust standard errors. With the covariates centered at a fixed reference point, \(x_{ap}\) standing for \(x_{ap} - x_{ref}\), its two stages are
\[\begin{align}
y_{ap} &= \underbrace{\beta_{00} + x_{ap}^\top \beta_{0x}}_{\text{baseline line}} + T_{ap} \underbrace{\left(\beta_{10} + x_{ap}^\top \beta_{1x}\right)}_{\text{treatment line}} + \varepsilon_{ap} && \text{second stage} \\
T_{ap} &= \gamma_{00} + x_{ap}^\top \gamma_{0x} + Z_a \left(\gamma_{10} + x_{ap}^\top \gamma_{1x}\right) + \nu_{ap} && \text{first stage for } T \\
T_{ap} x_{apj} &= \gamma^{(j)}_{00} + x_{ap}^\top \gamma^{(j)}_{0x} + Z_a \left(\gamma^{(j)}_{10} + x_{ap}^\top \gamma^{(j)}_{1x}\right) + \nu^{(j)}_{ap} && \text{first stage for interaction } j = 1, \dots, k
\end{align}\]
with \(k = 5\) covariates. Each account carries the inverse propensity weight \(w_a = 1/\hat e_{\text{day}}\) if prompted and \(w_a = 1/(1 - \hat e_{\text{day}})\) if not, where \(\hat e_{\text{day}}\) is the share of that day’s accounts that were prompted. One fit holds five outcome columns: hours \(y\), rebuffers \(N\), plays \(D\), and \(TN\) and \(TD\), which equal \(N\) and \(D\) for profiles with the setting on and 0 otherwise.
Stacking the instruments \(m_{1,ap} = (1, x_{ap}, Z_a, Z_a x_{ap})\) into \(M_1\), the regressors \(m_{2,ap} = (1, x_{ap}, T_{ap}, T_{ap} x_{ap})\) into \(M_2\), and the weights into \(W = \text{diag}(w)\), the coefficients are
\[\hat\beta = (M_1^\top W M_2)^{-1} M_1^\top W Y,\]
a \(2(k+1) \times 5\) matrix with one column per outcome, \(\hat\beta_y, \hat\beta_N, \hat\beta_D, \hat\beta_{TN}, \hat\beta_{TD}\).
The model rests on three assumptions about the design.
(A1) Accounts are independent of each other. Profiles of the same account may be correlated in any way.
(A2) Within a cohort, the prompt is randomized with probability \(e_{\text{day}}\), independently of everything else.
(A3) The prompt affects a profile’s outcomes only through \(T\), and no profile turns the setting on only when it is not prompted.

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
text:
The effects
The treatment line is fit to the compliers, so the effect for the compliers, the LATE, is the treatment line read at the compliers’ mean covariates \(\bar x_C\), estimated as a ratio of two intent to treat effects:
\[\begin{align}
\tau_{LATE} &= \beta_{10} + (\bar x_C - x_{ref})^\top \beta_{1x}, \\
\bar x_C &= \frac{E[T x \mid Z = 1] - E[T x \mid Z = 0]}{E[T \mid Z = 1] - E[T \mid Z = 0]}.
\end{align}\]
Write \(\ell_N\) for the treatment line of the outcome \(N\) read at \(\bar x_C\), and similarly for the other outcomes. Then \(\ell_{TN}\) is the compliers’ mean rebuffers with the setting on, \(E[N(1) \mid C]\), and \(\ell_{TN} - \ell_N\) is their mean rebuffers with it off, \(E[N(0) \mid C]\). The effect on rebuffers per play is
\[\tau_R = \frac{\ell_{TN}}{\ell_{TD}} - \frac{\ell_{TN} - \ell_N}{\ell_{TD} - \ell_D}.\]
The product manager’s question is about the relative change in rebuffers per play,
\[\rho_R = \frac{\ell_{TN} / \ell_{TD}}{(\ell_{TN} - \ell_N) / (\ell_{TD} - \ell_D)} - 1,\]
a third function of the same coefficients. The previous post computed standard errors with the delta method, which needs the gradient of each effect and the joint covariance of all the coefficients. Because we simulated the data, we know the true effects. We simulate the same accounts twice, once with every account prompted and once with none, and compare the compliers in the two worlds.


Code
truth_pair <- function(seed, n_accounts = 1e6) {
  set.seed(seed)
  p1 <- simulate_accounts(n_accounts, force_Z = 1)
  set.seed(seed)
  p0 <- simulate_accounts(n_accounts, force_Z = 0)
  C <- p1$complier == 1                                      # the same profiles comply in both worlds
  rate_1 <- sum(p1$N[C]) / sum(p1$D[C])
  rate_0 <- sum(p0$N[C]) / sum(p0$D[C])
  c(tau_LATE = mean(p1$y[C] - p0$y[C]), tau_R = rate_1 - rate_0, rho_R = rate_1 / rate_0 - 1)
}
truth <- colMeans(do.call(rbind, map(1:2, truth_pair)))
invisible(gc())
truth


   tau_LATE       tau_R       rho_R 
 0.61334648 -0.02724864 -0.37012026

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
text:
The compressed dataset
The previous post compressed the profile rows in two steps. Each account becomes an account summary \(u_a\), the vector of the sums over its profiles
\[S^Y_a = \sum_p \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ x_{ap} \end{pmatrix} y_{ap}^\top, \qquad S_a = \sum_p \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ x_{ap} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_{ap}^\top \end{pmatrix}, \qquad S^T_a = \sum_p T_{ap} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ x_{ap} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_{ap}^\top \end{pmatrix},\]
where \(y_{ap}\) is the row of all outcome columns. Accounts with the same prompt and cohort share \(Z_a\) and \(w_a\), so each stratum \(h = (Z, \text{day})\) becomes one compressed row with three fields: the number of accounts \(G_h\), the first moments \(\sum_{a \in h} u_a\), which give \(\hat\beta\), and the second moments \(\sum_{a \in h} u_a u_a^\top\), which give the cluster robust covariance. The compressed dataset has 8 compressed rows.

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
section: The unit that gets a weight is the account
text:
The unit that gets a weight is the account
The Bayesian bootstrap treats the population as a mix of the units we observed, in unknown shares, and draws the shares from their posterior. The unit has to be the unit of independence. Here that is the account, by (A1): profiles of the same account are correlated, so a population is a mix of whole accounts, each with all its profiles. We add the two assumptions of the bootstrap post at the level of accounts.
(A4) The population contains only the kinds of accounts we observed. Writing \(F_a\) for the population made only of copies of account \(a\), with its cohort, prompt, profiles and outcomes, the population is \(F = \sum_a \pi_a F_a\) for unknown shares \(\pi_a \geq 0\) that add up to 1.
(A5) The prior on the shares \(\pi = (\pi_1, \dots, \pi_G)\), where \(G\) is the number of accounts, is a Dirichlet distribution with zero pseudo-counts.
As the bootstrap post derived, the posterior of \(\pi\) is then Dirichlet\((1, \dots, 1)\), and a draw is
\[\pi_a = \frac{\xi_a}{\sum_{a'} \xi_{a'}}, \qquad \xi_a \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Exponential}(1).\]
\(\xi_a\) is the account’s bootstrap weight. It is a weight but not a probability weight; \(\pi_a\) is the probability weight. Every profile of an account shares the account’s bootstrap weight.

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
section: The effects as functions of the population
text:
The effects as functions of the population
To compute an effect on a drawn population, we write each step of the universal model as a function of \(F\). With \(F = \sum_a \pi_a F_a\), an average over \(F\) is a \(\pi\)-weighted average over our accounts.

The propensity. The share of a cohort’s accounts that were prompted is \[e_{\text{day}}(F) = \frac{\sum_{a \in \text{day}} \pi_a Z_a}{\sum_{a \in \text{day}} \pi_a},\] and the inverse propensity weights \(w_a(F)\) follow from it. Each draw of the population has its own share of prompted accounts, so the propensity is recomputed in every draw.
The coefficients. The universal model solves \(\sum_a w_a \sum_p m_{1,ap} (y_{ap} - m_{2,ap}^\top \beta) = 0\) on our sample. On the population \(F\) the sum over accounts becomes a \(\pi\)-weighted sum, so the solution is \[\beta(F) = \Big(\sum_a \pi_a w_a(F) \sum_p m_{1,ap} m_{2,ap}^\top\Big)^{-1} \sum_a \pi_a w_a(F) \sum_p m_{1,ap} y_{ap}^\top,\] which is the universal model fit with the combined weight \(\pi_a w_a(F)\) on every profile of account \(a\).
The compliers’ mean. \(\bar x_C(F)\) is the ratio of intent to treat effects, with each expectation a weighted average with weights \(\pi_a w_a(F)\).
The effects. \(\tau_{LATE}(F)\), \(\tau_R(F)\) and \(\rho_R(F)\) are the same functions of \(\beta(F)\) and \(\bar x_C(F)\) as before.

Every step is unchanged when all the \(\pi_a\) are multiplied by the same constant: the propensity is a ratio, and the constant cancels between the inverse and the second sum of \(\beta(F)\), and in the ratio \(\bar x_C(F)\). So we can use the bootstrap weights \(\xi_a\) directly, without normalizing them. With all \(\xi_a = 1\) the steps reproduce the estimates of the previous post exactly.
At the true population, \(\tau_{LATE}(F)\) is the LATE: the previous post derived that the treatment line is fit to the compliers’ effects under (A1)–(A3), and that derivation holds for any population that satisfies them. The posterior of \(\tau_{LATE}(F)\) is therefore a posterior for the LATE.

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
text:
One draw, step by step
draw_rows computes the three effects on the profile rows for one vector of bootstrap weights, one per account. It recomputes the propensity, refits the model with the combined weights, and recomputes the compliers’ mean. rows_data prepares the matrices once, because they do not change across draws.


Code
rows_data <- function(df) {
  accounts <- df |>
    distinct(account, day, Z) |>
    arrange(account)
  stopifnot(all(accounts$account == seq_len(nrow(accounts))))   # accounts numbered 1, 2, ...
  c(design(df), list(Y = as.matrix(df[y_cols]), r = centered(df), account = df$account, Z = df$Z, T = df$T,
                     accounts = accounts))
}

effect_values <- function(beta, x_C_c) {        # x_C_c: the compliers' mean in centered units
  delta <- c(rep(0, d), 1, x_C_c)
  l <- colSums(delta * beta)                     # each outcome's treatment line at the compliers' mean
  rate_1 <- l[["TN"]] / l[["TD"]]
  rate_0 <- (l[["TN"]] - l[["N"]]) / (l[["TD"]] - l[["D"]])
  c(tau_LATE = l[["y"]], tau_R = rate_1 - rate_0, rho_R = rate_1 / rate_0 - 1)
}

draw_rows <- function(rows, xi, ramp = TRUE, encouraged = TRUE) {
  acc <- rows$accounts
  # 1. The propensity: the xi-weighted share of each cohort's accounts that were prompted
  e_day <- rowsum(xi * acc$Z, acc$day)[, 1] / rowsum(xi, acc$day)[, 1]
  w <- if (ramp) if_else(acc$Z == 1, 1 / e_day[acc$day], 1 / (1 - e_day[acc$day])) else 1
  # 2. The coefficients, with the combined weight xi_a w_a on every profile of account a
  w_ap <- (xi * w)[rows$account]
  beta <- solve(crossprod(rows$M_1 * w_ap, rows$M_2), crossprod(rows$M_1 * w_ap, rows$Y))
  colnames(beta) <- y_cols
  # 3. The compliers' mean: ratio of the weighted intent to treat effects on T (1, x) and T
  x_C_c <- if (encouraged) {
    arm <- \(z) colSums(rows$r * (w_ap * rows$T * (rows$Z == z))) / sum(w_ap * (rows$Z == z))
    diff <- arm(1) - arm(0)
    diff[-1] / diff[1]
  } else colSums(rows$r * w_ap)[-1] / sum(w_ap)
  # 4. The effects
  effect_values(beta, x_C_c)
}

draw_rows(rows, rep(1, nrow(rows$accounts)))

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
section: Does the posterior agree with the sandwich?
text:
Does the posterior agree with the sandwich?
The posterior standard deviations in Table 1 are close to the previous post’s standard errors: 0.0583 against 0.0572 for the LATE, and 0.00424 against 0.00410 for the ratio. With 1,000 draws, a posterior standard deviation carries Monte Carlo noise of about \(1/\sqrt{2 \cdot 999} \approx 2\%\). Why should they agree?
The bootstrap post linearized a weighted least squares draw around the estimate and found the sandwich. The same argument works here. A draw is a smooth function of the weighted sums over accounts, and each weighted sum moves from its value at \(\xi = 1\) by \(\sum_a (\xi_a - 1) \times\) (the account’s contribution). To first order, an effect’s draw is
\[\tau^{(b)} - \hat\tau \approx \sum_a (\xi^{(b)}_a - 1)\, \psi_a,\]
where \(\psi_a\) is account \(a\)’s influence on the effect, the change in \(\hat\tau\) per unit change in the account’s weight. The bootstrap weights are independent with variance 1, so the posterior variance is approximately \(\sum_a \psi_a^2\), a sum of squared influences over accounts. The previous post’s cluster robust variance is also a sum of squared influences over accounts, with one difference: it held \(\hat e_{\text{day}}\) and \(\bar x_C\) fixed, so its \(\psi_a\) only describes how the account moves \(\hat\beta\). The bootstrap also moves the propensities and the compliers’ mean. Taddy et al. (2016) show the same first order equivalence for least squares in digital experiments.
How much do the extra terms matter? We rerun the same draws with the compliers’ mean held at its estimate.


Code
draw_fixed_x_C <- function(rows, xi, x_C_c) {
  acc <- rows$accounts
  e_day <- rowsum(xi * acc$Z, acc$day)[, 1] / rowsum(xi, acc$day)[, 1]
  w_ap <- (xi * if_else(acc$Z == 1, 1 / e_day[acc$day], 1 / (1 - e_day[acc$day])))[rows$account]
  beta <- solve(crossprod(rows$M_1 * w_ap, rows$M_2), crossprod(rows$M_1 * w_ap, rows$Y))
  colnames(beta) <- y_cols
  effect_values(beta, x_C_c)
}
post_fixed <- map(seq_len(B), \(b) draw_fixed_x_C(rows, Xi[, b], x_C - x_ref)) |>
  do.call(what = rbind)
rbind(`previous post: se` = c(css$se, NA),
      `posterior sd, x_C held fixed` = apply(post_fixed, 2, sd),
      `posterior sd` = apply(post, 2, sd))

Holding the compliers’ mean fixed brings the posterior standard deviation of the LATE to 0.0566, close to the sandwich. So the uncertainty in \(\bar x_C\), which the delta method of the previous post left out, accounts for the difference in this experiment. The appendix shows over 1,000 simulated experiments that the difference is small on average, and that both are calibrated. The bootstrap includes it without any extra derivation.

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
text:
Checking every design
The previous post showed that turning off the encouragement, the clusters or the ramp gives the textbook analysis of a simpler design. The posterior should follow along: with the encouragement off, the compliers are everyone and \(\bar x_C\) is the weighted mean of \(x\); with the clusters off, each account has one profile, so the bootstrap weights are per profile; with the ramp off, the inverse propensity weights are 1. Table 2 compares, for each of the 8 combinations, the posterior mean and standard deviation of the LATE with the estimate and standard error of the textbook model from estimatr, and the ratio’s posterior standard deviation with the universal model’s sandwich. Each posterior has 500 draws, to keep this check fast, so each posterior standard deviation carries Monte Carlo noise of about 3%.


Code
textbook <- function(df, x_C, clustered, encouraged, outcome, covs = x_cols) {
  df_c <- df |>
    mutate(across(all_of(covs), \(v) v - x_C[cur_column()]))     # coefficient on T is the line at x_C
  rhs <- paste0("(", paste(covs, collapse = " + "), ")")
  f <- as.formula(if (encouraged) paste(outcome, "~", rhs, "* T |", rhs, "* Z") else paste(outcome, "~", rhs, "* T"))
  estimator <- if (encouraged) iv_robust else lm_robust
  fit <- if (clustered) estimator(f, data = df_c, weights = w, clusters = account, se_type = "CR0")
         else estimator(f, data = df_c, weights = w, se_type = "HC0")
  c(estimate = fit$coefficients[["T"]], se = fit$std.error[["T"]])
}

check_design <- function(encouraged, clustered, ramp) {
  set.seed(7)
  df <- simulate_accounts(propensity = if (ramp) propensity else rep(0.3, 4), full_compliance = !encouraged,
                          one_profile = !clustered) |>
    prepare(ramp = ramp)
  x_C <- complier_mean(df)
  tb <- textbook(df, x_C, clustered, encouraged, "y")
  css <- effects(fit_rows(df), x_C, x_ref)
  rows <- rows_data(df)
  post <- map(1:500, \(b) draw_rows(rows, rexp(nrow(rows$accounts)), ramp, encouraged)) |>
    do.call(what = rbind)
  tibble(encouraged, clustered, ramp,
         textbook = tb[["estimate"]], posterior_mean = mean(post[, "tau_LATE"]),
         textbook_se = tb[["se"]], posterior_sd = sd(post[, "tau_LATE"]),
         ratio_se = css$se[2], ratio_posterior_sd = sd(post[, "tau_R"]))
}

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
section: The weight must go on the account
text:
The weight must go on the account
What if we ignore the clusters, and draw a bootstrap weight for each profile instead of each account? draw_rows can do that if we pretend that every profile is its own account.


Code
rows_profile <- df |>
  mutate(account = row_number()) |>
  rows_data()
set.seed(3)
post_profile <- map(seq_len(B), \(b) draw_rows(rows_profile, rexp(nrow(df)))) |>
  do.call(what = rbind)
rbind(`weights per account` = apply(post, 2, sd), `weights per profile` = apply(post_profile, 2, sd))


                      tau_LATE       tau_R      rho_R
weights per account 0.05830711 0.004242300 0.04483163
weights per profile 0.05348719 0.003958555 0.04141338


Weights per profile make the posterior of the LATE 8% narrower. Profiles of the same account share network quality and engagement, so they are not independent, and a population that mixes profiles freely is more certain than the data justify. This is the posterior counterpart of using a heteroskedasticity robust standard error where a cluster robust one is needed. The appendix confirms over 1,000 simulated experiments that weights per profile under-cover the LATE, while weights per account are calibrated.
The Bayesian bootstrap of the universal model is the universal model fit with one more weight per account. It gives a posterior for every effect of every design that the model covers, and for any function of those effects.

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
section: The compressed rows cannot be reweighted
text:
The compressed rows cannot be reweighted
The tempting shortcut is to apply the Bayesian bootstrap to the compressed dataset: draw one bootstrap weight per compressed row and refit. That would treat the 8 strata as the units of independence. A population would then be a mix of 8 kinds of strata, and the posterior would describe uncertainty about the strata’s shares, not about the accounts within them. Within a stratum, every account would always count the same, so the posterior would not see how much the accounts vary. By (A1) the unit is the account, and a compressed row has already added the accounts together.

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
text:
What one draw needs
Look again at what a draw computes. Each step of draw_rows adds up profile rows with the combined weight \(\xi_a w_a\), and \(w_a\) is the same for all accounts of a stratum. Grouping the profiles by account and the accounts by stratum, the sums of a draw are sums over strata of the stratum’s inverse propensity weight times
\[\sum_{a \in h} \xi_a \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ u_a \end{pmatrix}.\]
The first entry, \(\sum_{a \in h} \xi_a\), is the stratum’s total bootstrap weight, which gives the propensities. The rest is the bootstrap-weighted sum of the account summaries, which gives \(\beta\) and \(\bar x_C\), exactly as \(\sum_{a \in h} u_a\) gave them in the previous post. We write \(v_a = (1, u_a)\) for the account summary with a 1 in front. One draw needs one weighted sum \(\sum_{a \in h} \xi_a v_a\) per stratum. fit_sums computes the three effects from these 8 sums.


Code
fit_sums <- function(keys, sums, ramp = TRUE, encouraged = TRUE) {
  # keys: Z and day of each stratum; sums: one row per stratum, sum of xi_a v_a
  total <- sums[, 1]                                            # total bootstrap weight of the stratum
  e_day <- (tapply(total * keys$Z, keys$day, sum) / tapply(total, keys$day, sum))[as.character(keys$day)]
  w <- if (ramp) ifelse(keys$Z == 1, 1 / e_day, 1 / (1 - e_day)) else rep(1, nrow(keys))
  s <- colSums(sums[, -1] * w)                                  # all strata
  s_Z <- colSums(sums[, -1] * (w * keys$Z))                     # prompted strata
  i_Y <- 1:(d * o)
  i_S <- d * o + 1:(d * d)
  i_T <- d * o + d * d + 1:(d * d)
  block <- \(v, i, ncol = d) matrix(v[i], ncol = ncol)
  M1_W_M2 <- rbind(cbind(block(s, i_S), block(s, i_T)), cbind(block(s_Z, i_S), block(s_Z, i_T)))
  M1_W_Y <- rbind(block(s, i_Y, o), block(s_Z, i_Y, o))
  beta <- solve(M1_W_M2, M1_W_Y)
  colnames(beta) <- y_cols
  x_C_c <- if (encouraged) {
    s_0 <- s - s_Z                                              # unprompted strata
    diff <- block(s_Z, i_T)[, 1] / s_Z[i_S][1] - block(s_0, i_T)[, 1] / s_0[i_S][1]
    diff[-1] / diff[1]
  } else block(s, i_S)[-1, 1] / s[i_S][1]
  effect_values(beta, x_C_c)
}


The sums \(\sum_{a \in h} \xi_a v_a\) change with every draw, and the compressed dataset of the previous post kept only \(\sum_{a \in h} v_a\) and \(\sum_{a \in h} v_a v_a^\top\), which are the same for every draw. There are two ways forward. We can compute the weighted sums of all \(B\) draws in one pass over the profile rows. Or we can ask what the compressed dataset already tells us about them.

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
section: Exact: draw the weights during the compression pass

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
section: From the compressed dataset: the compressed row is the posterior’s moments
text:
From the compressed dataset: the compressed row is the posterior’s moments
Do we need a new pass at all? The compressed dataset of the previous post holds, for each stratum, \(\sum_{a \in h} v_a\) and \(\sum_{a \in h} v_a v_a^\top\). Given the data, the account summaries are fixed and only the bootstrap weights are random. The weights are independent, with mean 1 and variance 1, so
\[\begin{align}
E\Big[\sum_{a \in h} \xi_a v_a \,\Big|\, \text{data}\Big] &= \sum_{a \in h} E[\xi_a]\, v_a = \sum_{a \in h} v_a, \\
\text{Cov}\Big(\sum_{a \in h} \xi_a v_a \,\Big|\, \text{data}\Big) &= \sum_{a \in h} \text{Var}(\xi_a)\, v_a v_a^\top = \sum_{a \in h} v_a v_a^\top,
\end{align}\]
where the covariance has no cross terms between accounts because their weights are independent. The mean and the covariance of the weighted sums that a draw needs are exactly the two fields of the compressed row. The count \(G_h\) is there too, as the first entry of \(\sum_{a \in h} v_a\), since the first entry of \(v_a\) is 1. The second moments are not centered, because the randomness comes from the weights varying around 1, not from the accounts varying around their mean. Weights of different strata are independent, so the weighted sums of different strata are independent.
The compressed row has the first two moments of the weighted sums, but not their whole distribution. Each weighted sum adds up hundreds or thousands of independent terms \(\xi_a v_a\), one per account: the smallest stratum, the prompted accounts of day 1, has 412 accounts. By the central limit theorem, each sum is approximately normal. So we draw the sum of each stratum from the normal distribution with the compressed row’s mean and covariance, and push every draw through fit_sums. Only the weighted sums are approximated as normal. The fit, the propensities, the compliers’ mean and the ratios are computed exactly from each draw, so the posterior can still be skewed when the effects are nonlinear functions of the sums.


Code
posterior_compressed <- function(moments, keys, B) {
  # One normal draw of the weighted sums per stratum and draw: mean sum v_a, covariance sum v_a v_a^T
  draws <- map(moments, \(m) {
    root <- eigen(m$second, symmetric = TRUE)
    A <- root$vectors %*% diag(sqrt(pmax(root$values, 0)))
    sweep(matrix(rnorm(B * ncol(A)), B) %*% t(A), 2, m$first, `+`)          # B x (1 + q)
  })
  posterior_from_sums(keys, draws)
}

moments <- compress_moments(df$account, st$h[df$account], centered(df), df$T, as.matrix(df[y_cols]), nrow(st$keys))
map_dbl(moments, \(m) m$first[1])                                            # G_h, the accounts per stratum


[1] 7639 5321 2988 1014  412  634  981 1011


Code
set.seed(4)
post_compressed <- posterior_compressed(moments, st$keys, B)


The eigen call computes a square root of each stratum’s covariance. A Cholesky factorization would also work, except that \(u_a\) repeats the off-diagonal entries of the symmetric blocks \(S_a\) and \(S^T_a\), which makes the covariance singular.
The two posteriors come from different random numbers, so we compare them with \(10{,}000\) draws each, to keep the Monte Carlo noise of each standard deviation below 1%.

Figure 2: Quantiles of the posterior from the compressed dataset against quantiles of the exact posterior, 10,000 draws each. Points on the line mean the two posteriors agree.





Table 3 and Figure 2 show that the two posteriors agree. For the LATE, the posterior standard deviations are 0.0581 and 0.0587, and the quantiles fall on the line, including the tails. What the normal approximation drops is the third moment of the weighted sums. The Exponential(1) weights are skewed, with a third central moment of 2, so the exact sums lean slightly to the right, and the compressed dataset does not keep the third moments \(\sum_{a \in h} v_a^{\otimes 3}\) that would describe it. In our experiment this is visible only in the skewness column. The exact posterior of \(\rho_R\) has a skewness of 0.29 and the compressed one 0.18: most of the skew comes from \(\rho_R\) being a ratio, which the exact fit of every draw keeps, and the rest from the weights, which the normal approximation drops. With very heavy-tailed accounts, such as a few whales that dominate a stratum, the weighted sums are less normal, and Taddy et al. (2016) found skewed posteriors in an experiment with 13 million users. There the exact pass is the safer choice.
There is another way to read the compressed posterior. Drawing the weighted sums from a normal with mean \(\sum_a v_a\) and covariance \(\sum_a v_a v_a^\top\) gives exactly the same distribution as weighting each account by an independent N(1, 1) number instead of an Exponential(1) number, because a weighted sum of fixed vectors with normal weights is normal. That is a multiplier bootstrap with normal weights. Its weights have the same mean and variance as the Bayesian bootstrap’s, which is why the two agree, but a normal weight can be negative, so a draw is no longer a population. We use the Gaussian draws as an approximation of the Bayesian bootstrap posterior, not as a posterior of their own.

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
text:
Compute and storage
To compare the costs, we run the same simulation with a million accounts, and time the three ways to get 1,000 draws: refitting on the profile rows, the exact one pass, and the compressed dataset. Refitting on the profile rows takes too long to run in full, so we time 20 draws and multiply by 50.


Code
set.seed(1)
big <- simulate_accounts(1e6) |>
  prepare()
st_big <- strata(big)
t_rows <- 50 * system.time({
  rows_big <- rows_data(big)
  walk(1:20, \(b) draw_rows(rows_big, rexp(nrow(rows_big$accounts))))
})[["elapsed"]]
rm(rows_big)
t_one_pass <- system.time(posterior_one_pass(big, 1000, 1))[["elapsed"]]
t_compressed <- system.time({
  moments_big <- compress_moments(big$account, st_big$h[big$account], centered(big), big$T,
                                  as.matrix(big[y_cols]), nrow(st_big$keys))
  posterior_compressed(moments_big, st_big$keys, 1000)
})[["elapsed"]]
n_big <- nrow(big)
rm(big, moments_big, st_big)
invisible(gc())

       seconds = c(t_rows, t_one_pass, t_compressed)) |>

Table 4 shows the times on the machine that rendered this post, for 2,189,477 profile rows. Refitting on the profile rows reads all of them for every draw. The exact one pass reads them once, but multiplies every account into 1,000 sums. The compressed dataset reads them once and multiplies every account into its outer product, which here is cheaper, and its 1,000 draws then never touch the profile rows.
The two efficient methods also keep different amounts of data. Write \(q = (k+1) o + (k+1)(k+2)\) for the number of distinct entries of \(u_a\), as in the previous post, where symmetric blocks count once. The exact one pass keeps \(B (1 + q)\) numbers per stratum. The compressed dataset keeps the distinct entries of \(\sum_{a \in h} v_a v_a^\top\), which is \((q+1)(q+2)/2\) numbers per stratum, and it already contains \(G_h\) and \(\sum_{a \in h} v_a\) as its first row. The first grows like \(B k^2\), the second like \(k^4\).

With our 5 covariates, the compressed dataset keeps 21,608 numbers, while the exact one pass keeps 584,000, about as many as the 527,868 numbers in the profile rows of this experiment of 20,000 accounts. Neither grows with the number of accounts, so for an experiment with a million accounts both are much smaller than the data. The two cross near \(q = 2B\): with 50 covariates the compressed dataset keeps more than the exact one pass. With prognostic scores, the previous post’s recommendation for many covariates, \(k\) stays at one score per raw outcome, and the compressed dataset stays small.
The choice between the two:

The compressed dataset is the default. It is the same compressed dataset that the previous post stores for standard errors, so a platform that already keeps it gets the posterior for free, for any number of draws and any function of the effects, without reading the profile rows again. Its only approximation is the normality of each stratum’s weighted sum.
The exact one pass is for strata with few accounts or very heavy-tailed accounts, where the weighted sums are not normal, or when an exact posterior is required. It needs the number of draws, and the seed, before the pass.

title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
text:
Monte Carlo
We repeat the experiment 1,000 times. In each one we compute the previous post’s estimates and standard errors, and three posteriors with 500 draws each: the exact posterior with weights per account, from the one pass; the posterior with weights per profile, from the same pass with every profile treated as its own account; and the posterior from the compressed dataset. A 95% credible interval is the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the draws. A posterior is not required to cover the truth in 95% of experiments, but when the posterior’s spread matches the sampling variability of the estimate, as the linearization argument says it should, it does. The SE/SD column divides the average standard error, or the average posterior standard deviation, by the standard deviation of the estimates across experiments.


Code
analyze <- function(seed, B = 500) {
  set.seed(seed)
  df <- simulate_accounts() |>
    prepare()
  css <- effects(fit_rows(df), complier_mean(df), x_ref)
  st <- strata(df)
  moments <- compress_moments(df$account, st$h[df$account], centered(df), df$T, as.matrix(df[y_cols]), nrow(st$keys))
  posteriors <- list(
    "weights per account, exact" = posterior_one_pass(df, B, seed),
    "weights per profile" = posterior_one_pass(mutate(df, account = row_number()), B, seed),
    "weights per account, compressed dataset" = posterior_compressed(moments, st$keys, B))
  bind_rows(
    tibble(effect = css$effect, method = "previous post: estimate and SE", estimate = css$estimate, spread = css$se,
           lo = css$estimate - qnorm(0.975) * css$se, hi = css$estimate + qnorm(0.975) * css$se),
    imap_dfr(posteriors, \(p, name) tibble(effect = colnames(p), method = name, estimate = colMeans(p),
                                           spread = apply(p, 2, sd), lo = apply(p, 2, quantile, 0.025),
                                           hi = apply(p, 2, quantile, 0.975)))) |>
    mutate(rep = seed)
}
rm(Xi, post_fixed, post_profile, rows_profile)
invisible(gc())
mc <- mclapply(1:1000, analyze, mc.cores = cores) |>
  bind_rows()
mc_tab <- mc |>
  mutate(target = truth[effect]) |>
  group_by(effect, method) |>
  summarise(bias = mean(estimate - target), sd = sd(estimate), se_over_sd = mean(spread) / sd(estimate),
            coverage = mean(lo <= target & target <= hi), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(factor(effect, levels = names(truth)), method)
